Known-truth controls

Source: vignettes/controls.Rmd
controls.Rmd
library(masque)

Why

masque gives an analyst the structure of a confidential table without its values. A control is a copy of a table in which part of the answer is fixed by construction, so a pipeline can be run where the right reading is known.

  • The null control permutes every analysed column, so no analysed column is associated with another or with the treatment. It is a smoke test. A pipeline that finds strong signal on it has built that signal itself, from the outcome or from a column the shuffle left alone. A leak that sits in the table, such as a covariate that copies the outcome, is shuffled away with everything else, so a quiet null does not clear a pipeline.
  • The negative control permutes one declared column, by default the treatment, within the design strata. Its allocation is random within them and everything else is as it was, the outcome included. It is a sham assignment: the permuted column is unrelated to the outcome, and any real effect it had stays in the outcome as extra noise. Over many replicates the share of negatives on which a pipeline rejects is its false-positive rate on this table under this allocation. On a randomised experiment, the rank of the real result among them is a randomisation p-value.
  • The positive control adds a declared shift per level to the negative. The share of positives on which a pipeline finds it is its sensitivity to a clean shift of that size on this table.

In epidemiology a negative control is a variable chosen to share the bias of the question. These controls are null by permutation and share no bias, so none of them can show confounding.

Nothing is re-simulated. Each control is a permutation of the table it was built from, with a shift added for the positive. The design columns and the missing cells are those of the input, and every column keeps its set of values, apart from the shifted target of a positive.

A clone and a declaration

The example is the alpha-design trial shipped with the package: 24 genotypes in 72 plots, three replicates, six blocks of four plots within each replicate. The clone is made with mode = "local", because the plan in the last section asks for a conditional clone, which the default mode ("null") refuses. A local clone stays with the data owner. Here it stands in for the default or collaborate clone an analyst would receive.

trial <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "john_alpha.csv", package = "masque"))
r <- propose_roles(trial, mode = "local", detect = FALSE)
r <- set_role(r, c("rep", "block"), role = "design", action = "keep")
r <- set_role(r, "gen", role = "treatment", action = "keep")
r <- set_role(r, "yield", role = "outcome", action = "scramble")
r <- set_role(r, c("plot", "row", "col"), role = "id", action = "keep")
m <- mask(trial, r, mode = "local", seed = 1L)
clone <- synthetic(m)

The control spec is declared once, before any control exists. It names the column to permute, the strata to permute it within, the outcome to plant an effect on, the effect per genotype in units of the outcome’s standard deviation, the number of replicates and the seed. Here the planted genotype effects are drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation 0.5, under the spec’s seed, so the same vector is planted on every table the spec meets.

spec <- control_spec(
  on = "gen",
  target = "yield",
  effect = list(sd = 0.5),
  strata = "rep",
  n = 19L,
  seed = 2026L
)
spec
#> 
#> ── masque_control_spec ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • Permuted column (on): gen
#> • Planted-effect target: yield
#> • Effect (target-SD units): one shift per level drawn from N(0, 0.5^2) when the spec meets a table
#> • Strata: rep
#> • Unit of on: row
#> • Unit-grained columns: none declared
#> • Replicates: 19
#> • Seed: present

The analyst’s side: controls from the clone

The analyst holds the clone and its role table, and nothing else. The controls are derived from the clone, so they disclose nothing the clone does not.

ctl <- controls(clone, roles(m), spec)
ctl

The print shows the resolved declaration and the planted truth: for each genotype, the shift in standard-deviation units and the shift in yield units that the positive control adds to that genotype’s plots. The @truth table holds the same, and @manifest lists every dataset with its seed.

A small pipeline stands in for the analyst’s: an analysis of variance of yield on replicate, block within replicate and genotype, returning the p-value of the genotype term.

genotype_p <- function(d) {
  blocks <- interaction(d$rep, d$block, drop = TRUE)
  fit <- stats::lm(yield ~ blocks + gen, data = d)
  stats::anova(fit)["gen", "Pr(>F)"]
}

On the clone itself the genotype term is not expected to show, because the clone re-simulates yield without a genotype effect. On the null it should not show beyond chance. On the negatives it shows at the pipeline’s false-positive rate. On the positives it shows at the rate the pipeline finds the planted shift.

p_clone <- genotype_p(clone)
p_null <- genotype_p(control_table(ctl, "null"))
p_neg <- vapply(seq_len(spec@n), function(i) {
  genotype_p(control_table(ctl, "negative", i))
}, numeric(1))
p_pos <- vapply(seq_len(spec@n), function(i) {
  genotype_p(control_table(ctl, "positive", i))
}, numeric(1))
data.frame(
  dataset = c("clone", "null"),
  p_value = round(c(p_clone, p_null), 3)
)
#>   dataset p_value
#> 1   clone   0.563
#> 2    null   0.058
data.frame(
  controls = c("negative (19)", "positive (19)"),
  share_below_0.05 = round(c(mean(p_neg < 0.05), mean(p_pos < 0.05)), 2)
)
#>        controls share_below_0.05
#> 1 negative (19)             0.11
#> 2 positive (19)             0.21

The negatives give the pipeline’s false-positive rate, and the positives the rate at which it finds the planted shift. Both describe this pipeline on this table under these permutations, learned without a single real yield. Another table with the same design can give other rates.

The construction can be checked as well. The genotype means on a positive replicate, less those on its negative replicate, are the planted shifts exactly, because the two share one permutation. This checks the controls, not the pipeline: raw genotype means recover the shifts by construction, so only an adjusted estimate can show a fault in the pipeline.

neg <- control_table(ctl, "negative", 1L)
pos <- control_table(ctl, "positive", 1L)
recovered <- tapply(pos$yield, pos$gen, mean) - tapply(neg$yield, neg$gen, mean)
planted <- ctl@truth$shift_realised[match(names(recovered), ctl@truth$level)]
all.equal(as.numeric(recovered), planted)
#> [1] TRUE

The planted size is in units of the yield’s standard deviation in the table at hand. That standard deviation holds the block variance and any real genotype effect, so on the original a size of 0.5 is not half the noise the pipeline sees. On the clone, which keeps no block structure, the two nearly coincide. Read the size against the residual of the pipeline’s own model:

residual_sd <- function(d) {
  blocks <- interaction(d$rep, d$block, drop = TRUE)
  summary(stats::lm(yield ~ blocks + gen, data = d))$sigma
}
0.5 * ctl@truth$sd_y[1] / residual_sd(clone)
#> [1] 0.5109373

The owner’s side: the same spec on the original

The owner runs the pipeline the analyst handed back on the original table, and on controls derived from the original with the same spec. One thing changes: the permutations are drawn privately. Here that is an integer given as seed, which overrides the spec’s seed. The plan route below uses a 256-bit key instead. The planted vector still comes from the spec’s seed, so the truth is the same on both sides. A public seed would let anyone who knows the design, which the clone shares, rebuild every permutation and read the original outcome out of per-replicate results. An integer has at most 31 bits, so it hides the permutations only while nothing per-replicate is released.

ctl_owner <- controls(trial, r, spec, seed = 40371L)
p_real <- genotype_p(trial)
p_neg_owner <- vapply(seq_len(spec@n), function(i) {
  genotype_p(control_table(ctl_owner, "negative", i))
}, numeric(1))
p_pos_owner <- vapply(seq_len(spec@n), function(i) {
  genotype_p(control_table(ctl_owner, "positive", i))
}, numeric(1))

Before the owner’s usual output checking, each reading is classed by what it estimates. The false-positive rate over the negatives describes the pipeline under sham assignment. For a test whose null distribution does not depend on the yields, it says little about them. The rate at which the positives find the shift depends on the residual variance, so it tells something about the scale of the real noise. The permutation p-value, the share of negatives whose p-value is at or below the real one, is the result of the analyst’s test on the real table, and it goes through output checking like any other result.

data.frame(
  reading = c(
    "false-positive rate (negatives)", "planted shift found (positives)",
    "permutation p-value of the real result"
  ),
  value = c(
    mean(p_neg_owner < 0.05), mean(p_pos_owner < 0.05),
    (sum(p_neg_owner <= p_real) + 1) / (spec@n + 1)
  )
)
#>                                  reading      value
#> 1        false-positive rate (negatives) 0.05263158
#> 2        planted shift found (positives) 0.52631579
#> 3 permutation p-value of the real result 0.05000000

The owner’s readings describe the pipeline on the real table, and they are the ones that answer the analyst. The clone’s readings are a rehearsal. Here the false-positive rates are 0.11 on the clone and 0.05 on the original, and the positives find the shift at 0.21 and 0.53. The clone re-simulates yield without the block structure, so its residual variance differs from the original’s and the positives differ with it. A gap between the readings is a statement about the clone. Agreement is not a check on the pipeline, and a rate of zero on both sides agrees while saying nothing. The same planted 0.5 is 1.06 residual standard deviations of the pipeline’s model on the original and 0.51 on the clone.

The control tables built from the original hold the real values and never leave. Per-replicate results do not leave either: each replicate is one more query against the original, and with the permutations known they are linear equations in the real outcome. The replicate count in the spec bounds the queries for one pipeline, and every further pipeline or spec run on the original is another set of them.

Carrying the spec in a plan

So far the spec has been a separate object. A plan fixes it in advance, with the roles. mask() resolves it on the original and records it on the recipe. Where the unit or the strata are not declared, the plan picks them: here the replicate, since each replicate holds every genotype and a block does not. The clone is unchanged by the spec. Its conditional stratum is coarsened to the replicate, and the classed warning that says so is muffled here.

r_plan <- set_role(r, "gen", role = "treatment", action = "alias")
plan <- masque_plan(
  r_plan,
  conditional = "design",
  controls = control_spec(
    on = "gen", target = "yield", effect = list(sd = 0.5), n = 19L, seed = 2026L
  )
)
m_plan <- withCallingHandlers(
  mask(trial, plan, mode = "local", seed = 1L),
  masque_conditional_degraded = function(w) invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
)
recipe(m_plan)@plan@controls$default@strata
#> [1] "rep"

conditional = "design" keeps the design means and block variance and carries no genotype effect. A real effect moves into the residual, as it does when the owner permutes genotype for a negative control, so the clone stands in for those negatives. A fit on this clone does not show the residual of a fit on the original.

The analyst gets the plan in the clone’s own names and labels. handover() writes it to a folder with a default or collaborate clone, the data card and a note, and leaves the recipe out. From there the analyst rebuilds the declared controls.

analyst_plan <- clone_plan(m_plan)
ctl_analyst <- controls(synthetic(m_plan), analyst_plan)
ctl_analyst@spec@strata
#> [1] "rep"

The owner passes the same plan with the recipe and the real table. Cleaning is replayed, a table that does not match the recipe is refused, a spec changed since mask() is refused, and the permutations come from the digest of a key on the recipe, with no integer seed to search, so the analyst cannot rebuild them.

ctl_owner_plan <- controls(trial, analyst_plan, recipe = recipe(m_plan))
identical(ctl_owner_plan@seeds, ctl_analyst@seeds)
#> [1] FALSE

What a control cannot tell you

  • A kept column is structure and is never permuted. Leakage through kept columns, ids or row order passes the null.
  • The strata should let every level of the column reach every stratum, as complete replicates do. Permuting within incomplete blocks leaves each block with its own set of genotypes, so part of the real genotype signal survives on the negatives, and the false-positive rate reads high or low depending on the layout.
  • A sequential test depends on the order of its terms. A treatment entered before the blocks carries their variance, and its false-positive rate on this design is well above nominal. The negatives show this, as they should.
  • The negative control reassigns one column under exchangeable allocation within the strata. The outcome is unchanged, so a large real effect of that column makes the residual on a negative larger than on the original. It cannot detect confounding, and on observational data it is a permutation test with no randomisation guarantee behind it.
  • A planted effect is clean: the same shift for every plot of a genotype, no confounding, no interaction. The positives measure sensitivity to a clean shift of the declared size, not power against the real effect, and a pipeline that is biased under confounding still finds it.
  • A shift is added in units of the outcome’s standard deviation in the table at hand. That standard deviation includes the design variance and any real effect, so the same spec plants the same nominal size on the clone and on the original while the shift relative to the residual may differ. The @truth table records the standard deviation used and, as sd_within_strata, the standard deviation left after the stratum means are removed. That figure still holds the effect of on and any variance within the strata, so it is larger than the residual of a model that fits them.
  • Nothing is clipped. A negative shift can take a non-negative outcome below zero, and control_table() warns when it does. On a count the shift is added, not a change of rate.
  • A negative control estimates the size of a test that uses within-stratum contrasts, so fit the strata. On this design, with replicate strata, yield ~ rep + gen rejects near 5 per cent and yield ~ gen rejects almost never, because the replicate variance stays in its residual. A shared rate on both sides is agreement between them, and zero on both says nothing about calibration.
  • The null permutes the outcome across the whole table, so block and replicate means vanish and a mixed model sees a different variance structure. Calibrate false positives on the negative control, not on the null.
  • A pipeline adjusted until its controls read well has been fitted to this null and this planted shift. It can still be wrong for every other question.
